metadata.title: Comparing linear and nonlinear reading assessments in PIRLS 2016

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PIRLS 2016 and its ePIRLS 2016 extension, with multiple-matrix sampling and a rotated booklet design. The analytic sample is restricted to students who completed both the paper-based PIRLS and the digital ePIRLS assessments within each participating country/benchmarking entity. The manuscript does not report whether PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the bifactor IRT estimation, so weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text. For analysts working with PIRLS microdata, complex survey weights are typically required to obtain population-representative estimates under the multiple-matrix design; however, the paper’s modeling focus is on latent dimensionality (fit indices, ECV, reliabilities) rather than regression-based population means, so the practical impact of weights may be less central than for descriptive achievement comparisons.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are item responses modeled with IRT (dichotomized/rescored items), and the study does not use PIRLS/ePIRLS plausible values (PV) or report PV-based achievement outcomes. Because the analysis is based on item-level response modeling and the paper does not describe any explicit missing-item or missing-response handling rule, missing-data treatment is a reporting gap. This omission matters because multiple-matrix designs and item nonresponse can affect parameter estimation and fit statistics if not handled consistently.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used publicly available PIRLS 2016 data and included all 16 countries and benchmarking entities that took both PIRLS and ePIRLS 2016. Within each country/entity, the analytic sample was restricted to students who had taken both tests. For construct comparability, only the 85 AUI (acquire and use information) items from the PIRLS paper-based assessment were used (excluding the literary experience purpose), and ePIRLS contributed 90 AUI items. Partial-credit responses were rescored to dichotomous items (correct=1; incorrect/partially correct=0) before estimating the latent structure models.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (paper) + ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (digital), pooled across countries
main_findings.target_variable: Latent dimensionality of reading (general vs nonlinear-specific factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison via AIC/BIC: bifactor (S-1) best fit in pooled data (AIC: 276,868,789; BIC: 276,874,717) vs correlated two-factor (AIC: 276,988,499; BIC: 276,993,228) and unidimensional (AIC: 277,737,204; BIC: 277,741,920). Explained common variance (ECV): general factor ECV=0.870; nonlinear-specific factor ECV=0.120. Reliability: general factor RG=0.855; nonlinear-specific factor RN=0.504.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 AUI (digital) data pooled across countries, the study compared unidimensional, correlated two-factor, and bifactor (S-1) IRT models to explain item responses, finding that the bifactor (S-1) model best fit and that the general reading factor explained most variance (ECV=0.870) while the nonlinear-specific factor explained a smaller but nontrivial share (ECV=0.120). This indicates that nonlinear digital reading introduces an additional, partially separable skill dimension beyond general reading comprehension, supporting assessment designs that account for mode/structure differences rather than assuming full interchangeability.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS 2016 (paper-based linear reading) and ePIRLS 2016 (digital nonlinear reading) item-level data for fourth-grade students, restricting to the AUI purpose and to students who completed both tests. Across 16 participating countries/benchmarking entities, the authors estimate and compare unidimensional 2PL, correlated two-factor 2PL, and bifactor (S-1) IRT models using the mirt package in R. In the pooled analysis (n=85,075), the bifactor (S-1) model shows the best fit by AIC/BIC and yields a high general-factor explained common variance (ECV=0.870) alongside a smaller nonlinear-specific ECV (0.120), with general-factor reliability around 0.855 and nonlinear-specific reliability around 0.504. The paper also reports substantial cross-country variation in the nonlinear-specific ECV (e.g., ~0.050 in Singapore vs ~0.185 in Georgia) and notes that PIRLS design confounds delivery mode with construct structure, limiting causal interpretation of “nonlinear reading ability.”
